questions.enonce_markdown: Show that the equation of the normal to the hyperbola $xy = 4$ at the point $P\left(2t, \dfrac{2}{t}\right)$, $t \neq 0$ is $$t^3x - ty - 2t^4 + 2 = 0.$$
questions.corrige_markdown:
Write the hyperbola as $y = \dfrac{4}{x}$, so $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -\dfrac{4}{x^2}$. At $P\left(2t, \dfrac2t\right)$:
$$\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{4}{4t^2} = -\frac{1}{t^2}.$$
The gradient of the normal is the negative reciprocal, $t^2$. The normal through $P$ is
$$y - \frac{2}{t} = t^2\left(x - 2t\right) = t^2x - 2t^3.$$
Multiply by $t$ (with $t \neq 0$):
$$ty - 2 = t^3x - 2t^4 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \boxed{t^3x - ty - 2t^4 + 2 = 0.} \qquad \blacksquare$$
(Check: substituting $x = 2t$, $y = \frac2t$ gives $2t^4 - 2 - 2t^4 + 2 = 0$.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
The normal to the hyperbola $xy = 4$ at the point $P\left(2t, \dfrac{2}{t}\right)$, $t \neq 0$, has equation $t^3x - ty - 2t^4 + 2 = 0$. This normal cuts the hyperbola again at the point $Q$.

Find the coordinates of $Q$.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Let $Q = \left(2s, \dfrac{2}{s}\right)$ with $s \neq 0$, a point of the hyperbola. It lies on the normal when
$$t^3\cdot 2s - t\cdot\frac{2}{s} - 2t^4 + 2 = 0.$$
Multiply by $\dfrac{s}{2}$:
$$t^3s^2 - t - t^4s + s = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad t^3s^2 + \left(1 - t^4\right)s - t = 0.$$
This quadratic in $s$ has the root $s = t$ (the point $P$ itself): $t^5 + t - t^5 - t = 0$. The product of the roots is $\dfrac{-t}{t^3} = -\dfrac{1}{t^2}$, so the other root is
$$s = -\frac{1}{t^2}\cdot\frac{1}{t} = -\frac{1}{t^3}.$$
(This differs from $t$ for every real $t$, because $-\dfrac{1}{t^3} = t$ would need $t^4 = -1$.) Then $2s = -\dfrac{2}{t^3}$ and $\dfrac2s = -2t^3$:
$$\boxed{Q = \left(-\frac{2}{t^3},\ -2t^3\right)}$$
Check: $\left(-\dfrac{2}{t^3}\right)\left(-2t^3\right) = 4$, so $Q$ is on $xy = 4$.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The normal to the hyperbola $xy = 4$ at the point $P\left(2t, \dfrac{2}{t}\right)$, $t \neq 0$, has equation $t^3x - ty - 2t^4 + 2 = 0$. This normal cuts the hyperbola again at the point $Q$.

Prove that the locus of the midpoint of the origin and $Q$ is another hyperbola.
questions.corrige_markdown:
From part (i), $Q = \left(-\dfrac{2}{t^3}, -2t^3\right)$. The midpoint $M$ of $O(0, 0)$ and $Q$ is
$$M = \left(-\frac{1}{t^3},\ -t^3\right), \qquad\text{so}\qquad x = -\frac{1}{t^3},\quad y = -t^3.$$
Eliminate the parameter $t$ by multiplying:
$$xy = \left(-\frac{1}{t^3}\right)\left(-t^3\right) = 1.$$
As $t$ takes every non-zero real value, $t^3$ takes every non-zero real value, so $M$ describes the whole curve $xy = 1$ (both branches: $t > 0$ gives the branch with $x, y < 0$, $t < 0$ the branch with $x, y > 0$).

Hence the locus of $M$ is the hyperbola $\boxed{xy = 1}$, a rectangular hyperbola different from $xy = 4$ (it is the image of $xy = 4$ under the enlargement of scale factor $\tfrac12$ about the origin). $\blacksquare$
